newsitem.title: USA: A tale of two Md. counties divided on tax limits.
newsitem.headline: A tale of two Md. counties divided on tax limits.

text.p: Two adjoining Maryland counties passed vastly different tax initiatives in Tuesday's elections and their decisions will have repurcussions for debt offerings there, municipal bond experts said.

Prince George's County, Md., voters refused to repeal a 1978 property tax cap called TRIM, Tax Reform Initiative by Marylanders. On top of that, county voters approved a measure that mandates voter approval of all new taxes.
By contrast, voters in adjoining Montgomery County, Md., voted down a referendum proposal called the "Ficker Amendment" that would have required county officials to cut income or property taxes.
Bond market experts said the Prince George's County votes spell trouble for municipal bond issuance in that rapidly growing municipality.
"That's a big change. It's very restrictive," said Christopher Taylor, executive director of the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board on Thursday.
"Its going to limit issuance of tax exempt bonds in the county," he said.

Taylor said the Prince George's County votes are the latest in a string of tax limitation intiatives nationwide that grew out of "Proposition 13," the 1978 California vote to limit property tax increases.

The trend is sparking a new debate about whether such moves "are injurious to development and how a municipal jurisdication deals with restrictions on its tax revenue in a time of growth," Taylor said.
Similarly, an official for a local bond firm said, "It's going to have a negative impact on bond issuance."
"The county's got to collect revenues. If it is restricted as to how much it's collections can be, the bonds are not going to trade as well," said the dealer, who asked not to be identified.
Wayne Curry, Democratic Prince George's county executive who unsuccessfully called for repeal of TRIM, said he got the message from Tuesday's vote.

"The voters of Prince George's have spoken and spoken emphatically. They have called for a smaller, leaner government. And that's exactly what they will get," Curry said Tuesday, according to a press spokesman.
